concepts.name: Passed pawn
concepts.wording: A passed pawn: no enemy pawn ahead of it on its file or either neighbour, so only pieces can stop it. Its worth depends almost entirely on whether it can advance — a permanently blockaded passer is a liability rather than an asset.
cautions: PROVEN EXCEPTION to Tarrasch's 'rook behind the passed pawn': in the Vancura configuration — a rook pawn on the sixth with the attacking rook in front of it — putting the rook behind the pawn LOSES. Tablebase-verified on a pair differing only in the defending rook's square: beside the pawn is a draw, behind it is a loss in 63. See `vancura-position`.
A blockaded passer that ties down its owner's pieces is a liability, not an asset. Nimzowitsch's blockade rule is right about half the time, which is the honest figure.

concepts.name: Opposite-coloured bishops
concepts.wording: Opposite-coloured bishops: the bishops can never contest the same squares, so the defender can blockade on their own colour and the attacker's bishop can never challenge it. One extra pawn usually draws and two often do — on one wing. Passed pawns far enough apart beat a lone bishop, because it has to choose.
cautions: The drawish rule is an endgame rule. With queens and rooks on, opposite bishops favour the attacker.
Three files of separation between passed pawns usually wins despite the bishops.

concepts.name: Pawn break
concepts.wording: A pawn break: an advance into contact with an enemy pawn, played to open a file or a diagonal for the pieces behind it, or to force the opponent's structure to commit. It is not played to win a pawn.

A bad bishop defending a colour complex is doing essential work and should not be traded off casually.

concept.wording: A trapped piece: every square it can reach loses it just the same, so attacking it wins it. Not a pin and not a fork — the piece is free to move and has nowhere to go.

Returning the exchange at the right moment is a standard resource for the defender and must be accounted for.

Space bought by overextension is a liability — the hypermodern critique.

cautions: An isolated queen's pawn is not a weakness on sight. In the standard position measured here the side with the isolani is slightly better (+0.14).
The blanket rule 'trade pieces against an IQP' has an important qualification: trade MINOR pieces, but keep a queen and a rook, or there is nothing left to attack the pawn with.

why.point: Black is a pawn down on material, though the engine calls the position only level.

altConcept.name: Rook on the seventh rank
altConcept.wording: A rook on the seventh rank: it attacks pawns from a side they cannot defend and confines the king. It is decisive mainly when the king is trapped on the eighth behind it — if the king is out, the rook is good rather than winning.
cautions: A rook reaching the seventh is not decisive by itself. With an empty seventh rank and an enemy king that has luft, a tested position evaluates level at -0.04.
The king escaping forward removes most of the value at a stroke.

concepts.name: Fork
concepts.why: The queen on e2 forks the bishop on b2, the pawn on f2 and the rook on d1.
concepts.wording: One piece attacks two or more enemy units at once, so only one can be saved.
cautions: A fork wins nothing if the forking piece can be taken, or if every target is adequately defended and cheaper than the forker.
A relative fork can be met by a zwischenzug; an absolute fork cannot.

concepts.name: Pin
concepts.why: The pawn on f2 is pinned to the bishop behind it and cannot step aside.
concepts.wording: A pin. The pinned piece is stuck and makes a poor defender, so you can pile up on it.
cautions: A pinned piece still delivers check and still guards squares against non-king units.
A relative pin can be broken profitably when moving the front piece creates a bigger threat.

concepts.name: Hanging piece
concepts.why: It leaves the rook on d1 hanging — it can simply be taken.
concepts.wording: A piece that is attacked and can be captured for free — undefended, or defended fewer times than it is attacked.
cautions: A hanging piece may be a sacrifice offered on purpose. SEE says the material is winnable; it does not say taking is right.
In a lost position, giving material to reach a fortress or a perpetual can be correct.

concepts.wording: A piece that is attacked and can be captured for free — undefended, or defended fewer times than it is attacked.
cautions: A hanging piece may be a sacrifice offered on purpose. SEE says the material is winnable; it does not say taking is right.
In a lost position, giving material to reach a fortress or a perpetual can be correct.

concepts.name: Passed pawn
concepts.wording: A passed pawn: no enemy pawn ahead of it on its file or either neighbour, so only pieces can stop it. Its worth depends almost entirely on whether it can advance — a permanently blockaded passer is a liability rather than an asset.
cautions: PROVEN EXCEPTION to Tarrasch's 'rook behind the passed pawn': in the Vancura configuration — a rook pawn on the sixth with the attacking rook in front of it — putting the rook behind the pawn LOSES. Tablebase-verified on a pair differing only in the defending rook's square: beside the pawn is a draw, behind it is a loss in 63. See `vancura-position`.
A blockaded passer that ties down its owner's pieces is a liability, not an asset. Nimzowitsch's blockade rule is right about half the time, which is the honest figure.

concepts.name: Blockade
concepts.wording: Blockade: park a piece directly in front of an enemy pawn so it cannot advance. A knight is the ideal blockader because it keeps all its power from the square; a queen is the worst, because any minor piece evicts her.
cautions: A blockade that ties down a piece needed elsewhere is a liability.
Blockading with a heavy piece is expensive and usually temporary.

concepts.name: Bad bishop
concepts.wording: A bad bishop — its own pawns sit on the squares it travels on, so its diagonals are blocked from the inside and the squares they leave uncovered are ones the bishop cannot use either. The cures are a pawn break, a trade, or getting the bishop outside the chain.
cautions: Suba's active bad bishop: outside the pawn chain, a structurally bad bishop is often equal or better than a knight.
A bad bishop defending a colour complex is doing essential work and should not be traded off casually.

concept.name: Pawn promotion
concept.wording: Promotion: a pawn arriving on the eighth rank is replaced immediately, as part of the same move, by a piece of its own colour. The choice is free and unlimited — a side may have several queens — and it is not confined to pieces already captured.
cautions: Promotion is compulsory: a pawn may not remain a pawn.
Underpromotion to a rook avoids stalemate where a queen would cause it; underpromotion to a knight gains a check or fork unavailable to a queen.

concept.name: The principle of two weaknesses
concept.wording: A single weak point is holdable because every defender can gather around it. Fix it so it cannot be repaired, improve your own pieces while the opponent has nothing to do, then open a second front on the far wing. The defence cracks in transit between the two, not at either one.

Two weaknesses that the defending king stands between are not two weaknesses in the operative sense. Measured on the Lasker-Capablanca ending, moving the kings to d3/d6 costs the attacker over half the advantage.
